items.title: ‘Delhi became the source of all real knowledge’: How TV newsrooms pushed regional reporters aside
items.summary: Today, it feels as if the role of the reporter on a TV news channel has shrunk compared to the days when we started out. There are, of course, honourable exceptions, reporters who continue to produce high-quality work that makes an impact. But too many of the new crop of reporters deliver just what is expected of them—which is not enough in terms of originality and high standards. What is expected can, however, be too much in terms of working hours, number of lives or ‘OB’s. But with little reward in terms of the feeling of a responsible and important job well done, burnout is faster for the young reporter today. The initial thrill of coming on air and having access to the powerful can last a while, but is not enough to sustain them for a long career. A young reporter I worked with was very clear when she said, ‘I don’t want to be doing this when I am thirty!’ I had been on the job for more years than she had been alive, but I could understand where she was coming from. The devaluation of the field reporter has been a huge blow to the television news industry in India. I am talking about the genuine, around-the-year ground reporter—not the times when a Star Anchor makes the effort to come to the ground during election times or for very high-profile news stories—with the backing of a whole production team and their stories guaranteed air time in peak viewing hours. I am talking of the frontline person doing news reporting on the field. The one who is out there in the trenches, talking to the powerful and the helpless in this country of ours. I believe that a channel where a reporter is professionally respected, and given the logistical and editorial support to do the stories they need to do will be way ahead of others in terms of the quality of its journalism. Geography also matters. Across channels, Delhi began to play an ever-larger role in editorial decisions. With this change, there was angst in state bureaus over how often they were told by the Delhi news desk what story to do and how to do it—even though the regional reporter was really the one who knew the most about the situation. More and more, Delhi came to be considered the source of all real knowledge about a situation or news story—at least in the eyes of Delhi-based Senior Editors who were making the editorial decisions on how a story should be covered and played on air. This problem with the centralisation of decision-making and power is of course not restricted to TV news or even the media.

items.title: West Bengal SIR: Only 2% of 38 lakh appeals against exclusion decided so far; 91% of those names restored to voter rolls
items.summary: As of August 7, only 2% of the 38 lakh appeals filed by voters excluded from the electoral rolls prepared after West Bengal’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) have been decided by appellate tribunals since March 2026. According to a Right to Information (RTI) response from the office of the Chief Electoral Officer of West Bengal, of the appeals decided, 75,443 resulted in voters being included in the electoral roll, while 7,339 resulted in exclusion. In other words, 91.13% of the decided appeals resulted in inclusion. These voters were not allowed to cast votes during the recent West Bengal assembly elections. The RTI response was provided in response to Congress MP Isha Khan Choudhury's application. He had sought information on the appeals arising from the SIR exercise. The figures provide a district-wise and gender-wise picture of the electoral rolls alongside the status of the appellate process. The response shows that 37,27,838 appeals, or 97.83% of the total, are still pending, with only 1 in every 46 appeals decided so far. West Bengal SIR RTI report, Appellant Tribunal The numbers came up before the Supreme Court on Tuesday in a matter concerning the functioning of the SIR appellate tribunals. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana directed the Election Commission of India (ECI) to provide details of the pending appeals and the nature of the relief sought in them. The RTI response also showed how the SIR changed the size of West Bengal’s electoral roll. The State had 7,60,10,006 electors in the 2024 roll. By February 28, 2026, the final SIR roll had 6,44,52,609 electors, which is a fall of 1,15,57,397, or 15.21%. The reduction was spread across both male and female voters. Districts of Kolkata South and Maldah recorded the largest proportional falls, with their electoral rolls shrinking by more than 30%. items.title: Indian courts remain crucial for urgent relief despite rise of emergency arbitration: JSA Partner Dheeraj Nair
items.summary: Lawyers faced with an urgent threat to assets in India will still turn to courts despite the availability of emergency arbitration, JSA Partner Dheeraj Nair said on Thursday. Nair said that while emergency arbitration has gained recognition, an Indian court may still offer the quickest and most effective remedy when a party needs protection within a matter of days. “As a practitioner, the first thing that you will do is move to the Indian court, because you know that if it is a Friday evening also, perhaps by Monday morning, you will probably get the matter listed. But can an MCIA or SIAC give me an interim award or an interim order by Monday morning? I'm not so sure. So, practically speaking, we will still run to the court .” Nair was speaking at The Expanding Reach of Emergency Arbitration: A New Global Trend , a panel organised by the Mumbai Centre for International Arbitration (MCIA) and Drew & Napier as part of Singapore Convention Week 2026. Nair's comments came during a discussion on whether emergency arbitration can offer a genuine substitute for court-ordered interim relief. He said the answer would depend, among other things, on where the assets are located, against whom the order has to be enforced and which remedy is the most effective and quickest. Where an asset in India faces an imminent threat, Nair said he would be inclined to approach the relevant Indian court rather than first obtain an emergency order abroad and subsequently attempt to secure relief in India. However, he said emergency arbitration could work more effectively where the relief operates directly against a contracting party and does not require the assistance of third parties or state machinery. items.title: Husband and wife living in same house but different rooms not cruelty by itself: Karnataka HC
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently held that merely occupying separate rooms in the same premises does not, by itself, constitute matrimonial cruelty. A Bench of Justices DK Singh and H Shanthi Bhushan said that such separation can assume significance when viewed alongside the broader matrimonial history of a couple. The Court noted that the husband in this case himself had admitted that the parties had occupied separate rooms for a considerable period. “Standing by itself, such an arrangement cannot be treated as cruelty. The mere fact that spouses occupy separate rooms, without anything more, would not justify a finding of cruelty." It held that the separation could not be viewed in isolation and formed part of a prolonged matrimonial history involving repeated disputes, allegations of abuse, estrangement, an earlier matrimonial proceeding and the eventual failure of the relationship. The Court made the observation while dismissing an appeal filed by a man against a family court verdict which dissolved his marriage with his wife on the ground of cruelty and directed him to pay permanent alimony of ₹25,000 per month. The couple were married since November 11, 2001 and had two children. The wife alleged that the husband subjected her to physical, verbal and emotional cruelty, neglected her and the children, and displayed suspicious and possessive behaviour. She also alleged that he had distanced her from her family members and relatives. Although the parties continued to reside in the same building for some time, they occupied separate rooms and were, in substance, living separate lives. She eventually left the matrimonial home along with the children. The husband denied the allegations. He alleged that the wife was influenced by her parents and other relatives and was herself responsible for the deterioration of the matrimonial relationship. The Bench said that the wife's evidence regarding repeated quarrels, verbal abuse, emotional neglect, the husband's suspicious and possessive conduct, the parties living separately under the same roof, his alleged habits and failed attempts at reconciliation had to be assessed along with the husband's own admissions and the surrounding circumstances. items.summary: The Supreme Court has asked the Delhi police to respond to the bail plea filed by Athar Khan, an accused in the 2020 Delhi Riots conspiracy case. [Athar Khan v State (NCT of Delhi)] A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi issued notice to the police on August 19 on an appeal filed by Khan against the Delhi High Court’s July 7 judgment denying bail to him. Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi Khan is facing charges under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), the Indian Penal Code (IPC), the Arms Act and the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act. The case concerns the alleged larger conspiracy behind the North-East Delhi riots in 2020. The prosecution has accused Khan of managing the Chand Bagh protest site and participating in the alleged conspiracy. The trial court rejected his bail plea on January 29, following which he approached the High Court. The High Court held that the material against Khan, including chats recovered from co-accused Ovais Sultan Khan and the statement of protected witness “Pluto”, prima facie indicated his role as a key conspirator in the violence. It further held that Khan had failed to satisfy both the stringent threshold for bail under Section 43D(5) of the UAPA and the ordinary principles governing the grant of bail. Khan has now approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court ruling. He has sought bail on the grounds of prolonged incarceration, delay in the trial and parity with co-accused Shadab Ahmad. Khan has been in custody since July 2020. He has also disputed the evidence relied upon against him, pointing out that no weapon was recovered from him and no CCTV footage showed him participating in the violence. Athar Khan was represented by Senior Advocate Raju Ramachandran and advocates Fauzia Shakil, Ahmad Ibrahim, Varisha Sharma, Shruti Narayan, Aryan Deol, M Huzaifa, Ayesha Zaidi, Nida Khan Salim and Ujjwal Singh. items.summary: A Delhi court has convicted conman Sukesh Chandrasekhar of impersonating a sitting Supreme Court judge and attempting to pressure a judicial officer in a bid to get bail. Chief Judicial Magistrate Harshita Mishra of Tis Hazari Courts found Chandrasekhar guilty under Sections 170 (personating a public servant), 189 (threat of injury to a public servant) and 507 (criminal intimidation through anonymous communication) of the Indian Penal Code. The Court described the incident as an “absurd theatrical production” through which Chandrasekhar attempted to manipulate an ongoing judicial proceeding. “ In this most absurd theatrical production of his, where he impersonated a sitting Judge of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India to manipulate an ongoing proceeding, he did not merely cross the line; he leapt over it into the realm of fatal institutional overreach .” In April 2017, Chandrasekhar was in police custody in connection with a corruption case pending before special judge Poonam Chaudhary. items.title: Can IP suits be instituted anywhere because products available online pan-India? Delhi HC larger bench to decide
items.summary: Companies cannot institute intellectual property suits virtually anywhere in the country merely because products or advertisements are accessible online, the Delhi High Court recently said [HUL Vs Kwick Living]. Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhan i opined that internet cannot become a basis for companies to claim territorial jurisdiction anywhere in India for instituting IP suits. He made the observation while referring to a larger bench three questions concerning territorial jurisdiction in intellectual property disputes, particularly those involving online transactions. “ It is extremely important to point-out that, by reason of the advent of the internet and the accessibility of goods at any remote location via the world-wide-web, the principles of law in relation to territorial jurisdiction of courts cannot be so diluted or be made so vague that a corporation could sue in just about any location within the country .” The Court added that such an approach would throw the very concept of territorial jurisdiction of courts to the winds. Therefore, it referred the following three questions to a larger bench: - Whether IP suits are governed solely by Section 20 of the Code of Civil Procedure, by Section 134 of the Trade Marks Act or Section 62 of the Copyright Act or by an interplay of all those provisions and if so, how? - Whether a corporate plaintiff must sue only where its principal or registered office is located when part of the cause of action has arisen there. - What jurisdictional rule should apply to online transactions in IP disputes in light of conflicting approaches in earlier Delhi High Court judgments. Anup Jairam Bhambhani The case arose from a suit filed by Hindustan Unilever Limited (HUL) against Kwick Living (India) Private Limited. It alleged that the campaign targeted its Vim and Surf Excel products. The claims in the campaign were unsubstantiated and misleading, HUL said. Kwick Living objected to the Delhi High Court hearing the case. It argued that the Court lacked territorial jurisdiction. Both companies have their registered offices in Mumbai. items.title: Karnataka HC quashes criminal case against Coorg homestay owner booked for not reporting rape of US tourist
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently quashed criminal proceedings against a Coorg homestay owner who was accused of failing to report the rape of US tourist who had stayed at the homestay [ Palecanda Ponappa v The State of Karnataka ]. Justice M Nagaprasanna observed that two of the charges levelled under against the homestay owner were the Foreigners Act, 1946. However, this law was repealed over seven months before the alleged offence took place. The Court, therefore, held that these charges cannot stand. " The incident forming the subject matter of the present proceedings is alleged to have occurred on 12-04-2026 i.e, more than seven months after the repeal had taken effect ... Criminality cannot be conjured out of a statutory provision which had ceased to exist when the alleged act occurred ," the Court said. Justice M Nagaprasanna The remaining charge was under Section 239 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), which deals with the offence of intentionally failing to report crimes. The Court observed that this provision does not punish silence as such. Rather it deals with a failure to provide information that one is legally duty-bound to give. The Court further noted that Section 33 of the BNS fastens a duty on the public to report certain offences. However, sexual offences are not among the offences referred to in Section 33. The Court also noted that the legislature has expressly added a provision to in the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO Act) to make it mandatory to report child sexual assault offences. Other sexual crimes, however, have not been added to the list of offences that one is bound to report. "The Court cannot transplant that duty into a statutory field where Parliament has consciously not placed it," the Court added. The Court concluded that there was no legal duty fastened on a private citizen, like the homestay owner in this case, to report an incident of rape. It added that while some may expect the homestay owner to report the incident out of a moral obligation, such moral expectations cannot be grounds for a criminal case. " Morality may expect a citizen to speak; criminal law can punish his silence only when the statute commands him to speak. A moral expectation cannot, by prosecutorial alchemy, be converted into a penal obligation ," the Court held. items.title: Court fee in joint writ petitions payable 'per petitioner' if cause of action is individual: Bombay HC
items.summary: The Bombay High Court on Tuesday held that court fees for joint writ petitions filed under Articles 226 or 227 of the Constitution must be paid 'per petitioner' when individual causes of action are espoused [Satyam Surana v. Bombay High Court]. Justice Sandeep V Marne clarified that a single set of court fee suffices only when co-petitioners share a common or identical cause of action. “This facility of convenience made available to the litigants cannot be misused for avoiding payment of court fees,” the Court observed, Justice Sandeep Marne The clarification came after advocate Satyam Surana filed an application seeking a declaration that court fees under the Maharashtra Court Fees Act, 1959 must be levied 'per petition' rather than 'per petitioner'. Surana contended that the statute prescribes a fixed fee for an application or petition presented before the High Court and intentionally omits the phrase 'per petitioner'. He argued that demanding separate fees for each petitioner causes unnecessary financial loss to litigants. The Court applied the test of 'common interest' versus 'individual interest'. “In my view therefore, the key to the problem is to examine whether what is sought to be espoused is a 'common interest' or 'individual interest'. It is only in cases where a common cause of action is sought to be espoused that payment of a single set of court fees can be accepted even though multiple persons may join in a Petition,” Justice Marne said. The order clarified that litigants must pay separate court fees when the outcome individually benefits each petitioner like in cases such as service regularisation, pension claims or recruitment challenges. “Separate court fees under Court Fees Act is payable on a Petition filed under Articles 226 or 227 of the Constitution of India 'per petitioner' and not 'per petition' when individual causes of action of petitioners are sought to be espoused in the joint Petition,” the judge noted. The Court explained that joint petitions are procedural conveniences allowed to save paper, space, and costs but judicial concessions cannot compromise State revenue. “By permitting multiple persons to join in one Petition for saving cost, space, paper, etc., the High Court cannot cause loss to the State exchequer in terms of court fees,” the Court held. items.title: Agencies must unite to trace, deport foreign nationals with fake Aadhaar: Bombay High Court
items.summary: All government agencies must work together to detect and deport foreign nationals using fake or fraudulent Aadhaar cards, the Bombay High Court recently observed [State of Maharashtra v. Unique Identification Authority of India & Ors]. In two separate orders passed on July 27 and August 10, a division bench of Justices AS Gadkari and Kamal Khata emphasised the need for joint action. Justice AS Gadkari and Justice Kamal Khata The bench flagged a concerning pattern where foreign nationals have illegally infiltrated into India and fraudulently obtained basic documents. “Foreign nationals have illegally infiltrated India’s border and have fraudulently obtained basic documents to conceal their true identity and subsequently procured Aadhaar Cards to claim Indian identity. In a few cases, the investigating agencies have reported that such persons have engaged in alleged anti-national activities after securing these fraudulent documents, particularly leveraging the Aadhaar Card to claim false legitimacy as Indian citizens,” the July 27 order noted. The Court highlighted that this pattern reflected a critical gap in inter-agency coordination and document verification procedures. “The availability of Aadhaar Cards obtained through fraudulent means creates cascading vulnerabilities across identity, immigration, and security systems, necessitating urgent and coordinated institutional response. It therefore appears to us that there has to be a concerted efforts by all the State and Central Agencies to trace out and deport all such foreign nationals on priority basis,” the same order noted. The orders were passed in petitions filed by the State of Maharashtra seeking information under Section 33(1) of the Aadhaar Act to investigate illegal border infiltration. The UIDAI cited Section 29 of the Act, which prohibits the disclosure of core biometric and identity information. However, the High Court invoked Section 33(1), which permits disclosure when ordered by a High Court judge for criminal investigations. In one case, an Afghan national overstayed his tourist visa and procured an Aadhaar card to claim Indian citizenship. items.title: Punjab & Haryana High Court flags non-cooperation of police witnesses in NDPS cases, summons top cop
items.summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court on Tuesday summoned the Director General of Police (Law and Order) over repeated non-cooperation of official witnesses in the trials under Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act [Naseeb Singh v State of Punjab] Justice Sumeet Goel observed that official witnesses in NDPS cases, who in most cases are police personnel, consistently fail to appear before the trial courts to tender their evidence, despite the issuance of bailable warrants and even non-bailable warrants. The Court added that there are several cases where even bailable warrants remain unexecuted for extended periods, resulting in routine adjournments of trials under the NDPS Act. "This state of affairs reflects a deeply disturbing and systemic lapse in the prosecutorial mechanism, whereby the trial is stalled indefinitely due to the indifference or willful non-cooperation of official witnesses. Such conduct not only frustrates the right of the accused—whether incarcerated or on bail—to a speedy trial as enshrined under Article 21 of the Constitution of India, but also gravely undermines the administration of criminal justice," the Court said. The Court noted that the police often act with urgency when registering an FIR, and arresting the accused but once the case reaches trial, the same urgency frequently disappears. It underscored that the presentation of challan does not conclude a case but only marks the beginning of a duty to diligently prosecute the case. "When the process issued by the court, repeatedly, fails to secure attendance of official witness, the issue is no longer an isolated administrative lapse but reflects a serious institutional failure. Judicial time is being spent not on adjudicating the case, but on compelling the prosecution to perform its basic duty," it said. In the case pertaining to recovery of 2.48 Kg of heroin, the accused has been in custody since March 28, 2025. He added that despite repeated non-bailable warrants against the police witnesses, they have failed to appear before the trial court. items.title: Delhi High Court tells Centre to decide plea to set up National Nursing and Midwifery Commission
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has directed the Central government to decide within two months a plea seeking the constitution of the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission (NNMC) [ Indian Professional Nurses Association (IPNA) Vs Union of India & Anr ]. Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma passed the order while dealing with a plea by the Indian Professional Nurses Association (INPA) flagging concerns about the delay in setting up the NNMC, which was supposed to replace the Indian Nursing Council under a 2023 law. By its August 17 order, the Court has directed the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to address these concerns within two months. “This Court finds it appropriate to direct that the present petition filed before this Court be treated as a representation on behalf of the petitioner, and the respondents are directed to decide the same, within a period of two months from date, under intimation to the petitioner herein,” the Court said. Its plea noted that after the enactment of the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023, which came into force in 2024, an NNMC was supposed to replace the Indian Nursing Council when it came to regulating the nursing and midwifery education, training and professional practice in India. In this regard, the IPNA pointed out that the National Dental Commission, National Medical Commission, National Commission for Indian System of Medicine and National Commission for Homoeopathy have already been constituted by the government. items.summary: Supreme Court Justice Sandeep Mehta has asked Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant to appoint a Chief Justice from another State to head the Rajasthan High Court "with immediate effect". In letters dated August 2, August 10 and August 17 accessed by Bar & Bench , Justice Mehta has accused acting Chief Justice Sanjeev Prakash Sharma of manipulating case listings in favour of rich litigants and misusing his administrative powers ahead of his retirement, due later next month. Justice Sharma was appointed as Rajasthan High Court judge in November 2016 and transferred to the Patna High Court in 2022. When he sought repatriation on health grounds, the Collegium headed by then Chief Justice of India DY Chandrachud declined the request in March 2023 and sent him instead to the Punjab and Haryana High Court. In May 2025, a fresh Collegium resolution recommended his return to Rajasthan. He went on to become the acting Chief Justice, a post Justice Mehta's letter says he has now held "for more than last 10 months." Justice Mehta's letters draw on a recent Supreme Court observation made by a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi in an unrelated case. They had flagged a growing trend of judges passing orders for extraneous considerations on the eve of retirement, and judges attempting to "hit sixes" before retiring. items.title: NLSIU cancels 2026 convocation after students oppose CJI's presence
items.summary: The National Law School of India University (NLSIU), Bengaluru, has cancelled its 34th Annual Convocation for the graduating batch of 2026, which was scheduled to be held on September 12, citing “unavoidable circumstances”. The decision comes weeks after students and alumni raised objections to Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Bar Council of India (BCI) Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra attending the ceremony. NLSIU's Academic Administration team had informed graduating students on August 3 that September 12 was the proposed date for the annual convocation. However, a notice issued by the university on Thursday said the ceremony would no longer be held. “Despite our collective best efforts, due to unavoidable circumstances, we are unable to hold the 34th Annual Convocation,” the university said in its notice dated August 27. The university said all graduating students would instead be conferred their degrees in absentia, after due approvals from its governing bodies. Students will have the option of receiving their certificates by courier or collecting them from the campus. In absentia means the degrees will be formally conferred without the graduating students being physically present at a convocation ceremony. “The University will share a new form and the process with all graduating students to choose their preferred option later today,” the notice said. The cancellation comes against the backdrop of opposition among NLSIU students and alumni to the proposed attendance of CJI Surya Kant and BCI Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra at the convocation. The CJI is the Chancellor of NLSIU and awards degrees to graduating students at the university's annual convocation. More than 700 NLSIU students and alumni had objected to Mishra and CJI Surya Kant attending the university's convocation. They had also demanded an unconditional apology from the BCI to the student and faculty community of NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad. The opposition followed a controversy at NALSAR after the BCI, on August 13, moved to halt the enrolment of the university's 2026 graduating batch after students and faculty objected to the proposed presence of CJI Surya Kant at their convocation. The enrollment decision was subsequently restored. But why does he not meet us now?” This is the question Mahalakshmi, a sanitation worker with the Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC), poses to Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay as the sanitation workers’ protest in Chennai entered its eighth day on Thursday, August 27. Around 300 sanitation workers, most of them women, continued their agitation near the Allikulam court complex after barricades were erected to prevent them from proceeding towards the GCC headquarters at Ripon building on August 26. The major demands The workers are seeking a revision in their daily wages from Rs 762 to Rs 832, as well as permanent jobs for contractual sanitation workers. Other demands include a weekly paid day off, one-year maternity leave for women sanitation workers having a third child, menstrual leave for local body and rural school workers, a food allowance, and office space for the union inside the Corporation building. The union has also sought withdrawal of cases filed against workers and their leaders during a 2025 agitation . They are also demanding a direct meeting with Chief Minister Vijay, who holds the Municipal Administration and Water Supply portfolio. The Greater Chennai Corporation falls under the Municipal Administration department. The workers say they want to place their demands directly before the Chief Minister rather than meeting with officials and ministers. “We don't have any weekly offs or menstrual leave. From August 2025, sanitation workers in Chennai had staged a prolonged protest against the GCC’s decision to privatise waste collection. items.title: US religious freedom panel seeks to revoke Mohan Bhagwat's visa
items.summary: Follow TNM’s WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) has expressed concern over Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat’s visit to the United States. It has urged the US government to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials allegedly linked to religious freedom violations. Bhagwat is currently visiting the US and is scheduled to speak at an event in New York City on Saturday, August 29. The report identified the RSS as the ideological parent of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). “We urge the US government to consider targeted sanctions against RSS members and Indian officials complicit in religious freedom violations, including revoking the visa issued to Mohan Bhagwat,” USCIRF Chair Asif Mahmood said in a statement on Wednesday, August 26. The RSS said in May that it had organised foreign visits to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary organisation involved in attacks on minorities. The report also said the RSS is a powerful Hindu organisation from which Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s BJP emerged. USCIRF is a bipartisan US government body that monitors religious freedom globally and makes policy recommendations. Its recommendations are not binding, and Washington has not imposed sanctions following recent recommendations from the commission. The US panel said members of RSS subgroups have perpetrated violent attacks against religious minorities, including Christians, Dalits, Muslims and Sikhs. It also alleged that policies under the BJP-led government closely align with the RSS’ Hindutva ideology and discriminate against religious minority communities. USCIRF’s 2026 Annual Report recommended that the US Department of State designate India as a Country of Particular Concern (CPC), citing what it described as systematic, ongoing and egregious religious freedom violations. The commission also highlighted religious freedom conditions in India during a May 2026 hearing.
